On this basis, Wolpe argues that, by the 1970s and 1980s, the balance in the relationship between apartheid and capitalism had shifted from the functional to the contradictory pole. More specifically, the rapid growth in the manufacturing industry under NP rule made South African capitalism heavily dependent on an increasingly educated and skilled Black working class based in the cities.

Writing about New Orleans since the Hurricane Katrina catastrophe of August 2005, Reed highlights one key difference:

It may seem ironic because of how the visual imagery of dispossession and displacement after Katrina came universally to signify the persistence of racial injustice, but a generally unrecognized feature of the post-Katrina political landscape

That is, or should be, an unsurprising outcome four decades after racial transition in local government and the emergence and consolidation of a strong black political and business class, increasingly well incorporated into the structures of governing. . . . And generational succession has brought to prominence cohorts among black and white elites who increasingly have attended the same schools; lived in the same neighbourhoods; participated in the same voluntary associations; and share cultural and consumer tastes, world-views, and political and economic priorities. (Reed, 2022: 239–240)

[T]he core of the Jim Crow order was a class system rooted in employment and production relations that were imposed, stabilized, regulated, and naturalized through a regime of white supremacist law, practice, custom, rhetoric, and ideology. Defeating the white supremacist regime was a tremendous victory for social justice and egalitarian interests. At the same time, that victory left the undergirding class system untouched and in practical terms affirmed it. (ibid.)

One key sign of the persistence of the ‘undergirding class system’ is the role that the Black middle class plays in politically managing especially in the urban United States (New Orleans is but one example). As Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor points out, ‘[T]oday, when poor or working-class Black people experience hardship, that hardship is likely being overseen by an African American in some position of authority’ (ibid.). , class exploitation and racial oppression mutually reinforce each other, as the COVID-19 pandemic has shown. Using level of educational attainment as a proxy for social class, one study found that, in the United States, working-class people aged between 25 and 64 were five times as likely to die of COVID-19 as college graduates. Only 5% of the deaths in the first year of the pandemic were among white college graduates aged 25 to 64, even though they were ‘more than one quarter of the study population. . . . In contrast Hispanic and Black working-class men comprised only 8% of the 25–64 year old population, but they were 29% of the premature COVID-19 decedents’ (Pathak, 2021: 13).

Indeed, the most profound contradiction is perhaps inherent – that between an economic system that is dynamic and mobile, with the search for profit, as Marx and Engels emphasise in the Communist Manifesto, subverting existing hierarchies and transgressing frontiers, and forms of racial oppression that, whatever their variations, identify some groups of human beings as inherently inferior to others. Maybe we see here at work the double movement of deterritorialisation and reterritorialisation that Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari argue is inherent in capitalism as a distinctive social form:

Under the first aspect, capitalism never ceases to surpass its own limits, always deterritorializing further, ‘extending itself in a cosmopolitan energy that overturns every barrier and every bond’; but, under the second aspect, strictly complementary, capitalism never ceases to have limits and barriers that are internal to it, immanent, and that, precisely because they are immanent never allow themselves to be overcome except by reproducing themselves on an enlarged scale (always more reterritorializing, local, global and planetary). (Deleuze and Guattari, 1973: 309)12
